en: Now, let's next have a look at a couple of
examples for one-argument functions.
For example, here I have a log function
which simply wraps the built-in console.log
method.
Now, we can argue whether such a function
makes too much sense, but we could be doing
that if we want the option of quickly
swapping console.log for some other
outputting or logging mechanism.
Then having our own logging function which
we use throughout our program could make
sense because if we ever switch from
console.log to some other mechanism, we only
need to make that switch in one place
instead of in multiple places.
And then we have a function where it makes a
lot of sense that we need one argument and
just one argument, and that would be the
message which should be logged.
Now, we could also come up with a way of
writing this such that no arguments are
needed, again, by creating a class which
takes the message in the constructor and
then has a no-parameter
log method,
but I'm not too sure whether this really is
an improvement.
It's a lot of extra code and we just replace
a function where it was totally obvious that
we might have
a parameter and where the kind and value of
that parameter also is no surprise at all.
So here I'm absolutely not a fan of changing
this just for the sake of changing it.
Instead, I think the original example with
one argument here makes a lot of sense and
is absolutely something we can keep around.
Now, here are more functions where one
argument makes a lot of sense and is totally
obvious.
For example, this square function, which
simply squares a number and therefore takes
that number as a single parameter.
Or the emailIsValid function, which takes
the email address which should be validated
as an input.
These are all examples for functions which
we can leave like that and where having one
argument is totally fine, obvious, easy to
read, and easy to understand.
